I'll start by reading the task file.

# Your task (after reading)

You are a student reader helping an editor test a teaching article before it is published.
Work only inside this directory. Do not search the web. Be honest: the editor needs to know
where the article fails to teach.

1. Read `article.md` from start to finish. The series has a glossary, `glossary.md`; look terms up there as a reader would, and report in your feedback only terms that neither the article nor the glossary explains.
2. Answer the questions in its "Check your understanding" section. Write the answers to
   `answers.md`, numbered like the questions. Two to six sentences each, in your own words; show
   working where a question asks for a calculation or a translation. After each answer add a line
   `Confidence: N` with N from 1 (guessing) to 5 (certain).
3. Write `feedback.md` with these sections:
   - **Passages I had to read twice**: quote each (one or two sentences) and say what was unclear.
   - **Terms used before they were explained, or never explained**: one line each.
   - **Claims I could not verify from the article itself**: quote each and say what evidence or
     step is missing.
   - **Section scores**: for each numbered section, a score from 1 (lost) to 5 (clear) and one
     sentence of reason.
   - **Questions that the article did not let me answer**: which quiz questions, if any, could not
     be answered from the text, and what was missing.
   - **One thing to add and one thing to cut**.
4. Write `diary.md`: a work diary of this session in the format of `diary-format.md`, with one
   step for reading, one for the quiz and one for the feedback. Record what was hard.

Finish by replying with one line: DONE.

# 10. Architecture and a Roadmap

The previous articles each examined one part of the system. This one puts the parts together. It takes stock of what the firmware now contains, describes four structural changes that the earlier articles imply but did not develop, and then orders all of the proposed work by cost, risk and what each step makes possible. By the end you should be able to say how many execution mechanisms the device carries and which could go, explain why one description of the reactor's functions should generate the three lists that are now written by hand, state what a typed binary screen protocol would replace, and defend an order of work from the evidence in this issue.

The article uses the vocabulary of the whole issue; every term is in the glossary. The most frequent are these. A *world* is one scheduled program, and the *nucleus* is the kernel that runs worlds. An *engine* executes a world's code: QuickJS interprets JavaScript, WAMR interprets WebAssembly, and the native loader runs RV32 machine code from ELF files. CJI is the project's first compiler, for unannotated JavaScript; the *typed compiler* is the second, for a small language with declared types. A *reactor* is the prebuilt C module through which a compiled application calls the system.

## 10.1 What the firmware contains

After two days of rapid work the device carries more machinery than any one design would have chosen.

| Component | Role | Size or extent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| QuickJS | Runs JavaScript worlds; also runs the typed compiler | Part of the base firmware |
| WAMR | Runs WebAssembly worlds | Part of the base firmware |
| Native loader | Loads RV32 ELF modules | Small |
| CJI runtime | Dynamic values, strings and a garbage collector for CJI-compiled worlds | Linked into the firmware |
| CJI compiler tool | CJI itself, compiled to RV32, for compiling on the device | about 660 kB in the image; relocated at boot |
| Typed compiler | Frontend, WebAssembly linker, RV32 lowering | 43 kB of JavaScript source |
| Shared typed reactor | Connects a fully typed application to the nucleus | 508 lines of C |
| Per-application reactors | Hold the parts of Agenda and Files that are not yet typed | 869 and 334 lines of C |
| Compositor | The world that draws every screen | 485 lines of JavaScript, compiled by CJI for the firmware |

That is three engines, two compilers, a run-time system that exists only for the first compiler's output, and three reactors. Each was a reasonable step. Together they are a cost in flash, in boot time and in the number of things a maintainer must understand.

A second inventory is as telling. The Editor exists twice: as 316 lines of JavaScript, which is the original and the reference for tests, and as about 1,730 lines of typed source. Agenda is 307 lines of JavaScript, and its typed version is 468 lines of typed source plus 869 lines of C. The typed versions are four to six times longer than the programs they replace: a factor of 5.5 for Editor, and 4.4 for Agenda when its C reactor is counted. The difference is the price of the language's missing features: no allocation, no string operations beyond single code units, and no `await` (Articles 8 and 9). With twelve applications still to port, that multiplier is the main argument for extending the language before porting further.

## 10.2 One description of the reactor's functions

A typed application reaches the system through 28 functions that the shared reactor provides. Each is currently declared in three places that must agree.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    I["One interface description (proposed)"] -.-> A
    I -.-> B
    I -.-> C
    A["compiler/typed-world.js: name, parameter types, result type, in order"]
    B["sdk/typed/rv32-slot.S: one jump per function, in the same order"]
    C["sdk/typed/world.c: the C implementation of each function"]
    A --- B --- C
```

The compiler's table gives each function's name and types and fixes its position. The assembly file lists one trampoline per function in the same order; native code calls function number *k* by jumping to the *k*-th entry. The C file implements them. The number of functions is also stored in a header at the start of the reactor's code area, and the linker compares it with the length of the compiler's table. That check catches a function added to one list and not the other. It cannot catch two lists of the same length in different orders. If the order in the first two files ever differs, calls go to the wrong function with arguments of the wrong meaning, and no check detects it.

The remedy is an **interface description**: one file that states, for each function, its name, parameter types and result type, from which a build step generates the compiler's table, the trampolines and the C prototypes. If the JavaScript version of the reactor proposed in section 10.4 is built, its function list is generated from the same file. This is ordinary practice wherever two languages meet. The WebAssembly Component Model's interface language, WIT, is a current example and has a useful property for this system: it can declare a *resource* type, an entity "that can only be passed around indirectly via handle values", with owned and borrowed handles. Handle types of that kind would express whether a handle argument is consumed or only lent (Article 9). Two further facts that Articles 7 and 9 need for each function are not part of WIT and would be this project's own additions to the description: which capability the function requires, and how much fuel, the counter that bounds a handler's running time, a call should be charged.

This change is small, and it is a precondition for growing the set of reactor functions safely, which every ported application will require.

## 10.3 A typed screen protocol

Article 2 presented evidence that the compositor is the largest consumer of time on the path to the screen, and noted that in the measured firmware it was already native code. The cost lies in what the compositor is asked to do. It is worth following one screen update through the system as it works today.

1. The application builds a description of its screen as JSON text. In the typed language this is done by writing string fragments into a buffer one after another; Editor contains 104 such `writeLiteral` calls, for instance `output.writeLiteral(at, ",\"color\":\"accent\"}")`.
2. The reactor converts the buffer from UTF-16 to UTF-8, escaping characters as JSON requires. The design notes budget up to six output bytes per input unit for this step.
3. The nucleus copies the message to the compositor's queue. A message is limited to 16 KiB. (This step would remain with any protocol.)
4. The compositor parses the JSON text into a tree of dynamically typed objects, which are allocated on a garbage-collected heap.
5. The compositor walks the tree, computes positions, and draws. (This step is the compositor's actual job and would remain.)

Steps 1, 2 and 4 exist only because the two sides exchange text. The figure of six bytes per unit in step 2 is from the Editor's capacity design note in the project's records. Both sides know the structure in advance: a screen is a list of rows, each with a style, an indentation and a run of characters.

A **typed binary protocol** states that structure once, as record layouts, and both sides use it directly. The application writes fields at fixed offsets, which the typed language already does for its own records. The compositor reads the same fields at the same offsets. Nothing is formatted, escaped or parsed, and nothing is allocated to hold a tree. A full Editor screen is 17 rows of at most 49 characters. As 16-bit code units that is 833 × 2 = 1,666 bytes of text, and with a four-byte header per row for style, indentation and length, 1,734 bytes in all.

The layouts belong in the interface description of section 10.2, so that the application's compiler and the compositor are generated from the same source and cannot disagree.

The natural companion is a compositor written in the typed language. The compositor is today 485 lines of JavaScript compiled by CJI, with CJI's run-time system behind it. A typed compositor would have no garbage collector and no dynamic values, and it is the one world whose speed every other world's responsiveness depends on.

This is the largest single piece of work proposed in this issue, and it rests on a hypothesis. It should be started only if the key-to-pixel measurement of Article 2 confirms that the compositor dominates.

## 10.4 One source for both engines

When the typed compiler fails or is disabled, the firmware falls back to the original JavaScript application. Every ported application is therefore maintained in two forms, and the two can drift apart. The tests rely on the JavaScript original as the definition of correct behaviour, which is appropriate during a port and becomes a burden afterwards.

The typed source looks like JavaScript with annotations. Could QuickJS run it directly? Two developments in the JavaScript world suggest the shape of an answer.

The first is **asm.js**, a strict subset of JavaScript designed as a compilation target. Its insight was that type information can be written in valid JavaScript: a parameter is given the type *integer* "by means of an explicit coercion on function entry", written `x = x|0`, and a floating-point type by `x = +x` [Herman et al. 2014]. Code in this style runs unchanged in any JavaScript engine and can also be compiled ahead of time using plain machine integers. Because asm.js is a subset of JavaScript, an asm.js program means exactly what JavaScript says it means. The asm.js specification adds only the rules for recognizing which programs are in the subset.

The second is **erasable type syntax**. TypeScript 5.8 added an option that rejects every TypeScript construct with run-time behaviour, so that what remains can be turned into JavaScript by deleting the annotations, and a proposal before the JavaScript standards committee would have engines ignore annotations as if they were comments. That proposal is at stage 1 of the committee's process, which means it is under consideration and nothing has been accepted.

For the typed language, deletion alone is not enough, because its semantics differ from JavaScript's in specific, enumerable ways.

| Construct | Typed language | JavaScript after deleting annotations | What a JavaScript emitter must add |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `a + b` on `i32` | Wraps at 32 bits | 64-bit floating point | `(a + b) | 0` |
| `a * b` on `i32` | Wraps at 32 bits | May lose low bits above 2⁵³ | `Math.imul(a, b)` |
| `a / b` on `i32` | Truncates; traps on zero | Fractional result; infinity on zero | A checked helper |
| `s.charCodeAt(i)` out of range | Traps | Returns NaN | A wrapper class with a checked method |
| `record` declarations | Fixed layout in memory | Not JavaScript | An object or typed array |

Each row is a mechanical rewrite. A third, small backend that emits JavaScript with these rewrites, together with a JavaScript implementation of the reactor's 28 functions, would let QuickJS execute the same typed source. The project's device-language study considered compiling the typed language to JavaScript as the way to *run applications fast*, and rejected it for that purpose, because the interpreter would still treat every number as a general value. The two purposes proposed here do not depend on speed.

- **One source per application.** After a port is accepted, the JavaScript original can be retired. The fallback is the same program in another engine.
- **A reference for the compiler.** The JavaScript emitter is a second, independent implementation of the language's semantics. Running an application through both and comparing screens is a test of the WebAssembly and RV32 backends that needs no hand-written original.

One limit should be stated. A reference derived from the same source cannot reveal an error in the source's logic. During a port, the original JavaScript application remains the standard of behaviour.

## 10.5 Fewer engines

Which mechanisms of section 10.1 are needed in the long run depends on the outcome of earlier articles' proposals.

| Component | Needed as long as | Could be removed when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| QuickJS | Unported JavaScript worlds exist; it also hosts the typed compiler and the interactive console | Not in view; it is the system's base |
| WAMR | Typed applications from untrusted source must be confined | The verifier of Article 7 exists and is trusted, and no foreign WebAssembly modules are wanted |
| CJI runtime | Any CJI-compiled world ships, which today includes the compositor and the drivers | Those worlds are ported to the typed language |
| CJI compiler tool on the device | Compiling unannotated JavaScript on the device remains a goal | Now, by giving up that goal. Its build times of minutes make it unusable interactively, and it costs 660 kB and a boot-time relocation that had to be scheduled around |
| Per-application reactors | Agenda and Files keep logic in C | Those applications are fully typed |

The clearest decision is the fourth row. CJI remains valuable as a workstation compiler that turns existing JavaScript worlds into native code for the firmware image, and the techniques of Article 4 would improve it in that role. As the compiler that runs on the device, it has been superseded by the typed compiler.

## 10.6 The roadmap

The table gathers every proposal in this issue. Effort is a rough class: small is days, medium is one to two weeks, large is more. "Unlocks" names what becomes possible afterwards.

| # | Step | Effort | Risk | Unlocks | Article |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| 0 | Measure key press to pixels, and per-world time for one key press | small | low | Every later decision | 2 |
| 1 | Cache compiled modules under a content key | small | low | Removes 2–3 s from every boot | 6 |
| 2 | Take the CJI tool off the device | small | low | 660 kB of flash; simpler boot | 10 |
| 3 | Interface description for reactor functions | small | low | Safe growth of the reactor; data for steps 6 and 8 | 10 |
| 4 | Language: enumerations, distinct integers, guard facts for bounds checks, a report of reactor usage per world, `else`, `for`, `break`, forward calls with a cycle check | small each | low | Shorter, safer typed sources; fewer checks | 9 |
| 5 | RV32 backend with a compile-time operand stack | medium | medium | Native code about 2.7 times smaller; memory headroom | 5 |
| 6 | Fuel counter, static stack bound, output verifier | medium | medium | Native code from untrusted source | 7 |
| 7 | `await` compiled to state machines | medium to large | medium | Ports without hand-written continuations | 8 |
| 8 | Per-turn arena with its lifetime rules | medium | medium | Applications that allocate | 9 |
| 9 | JavaScript emitter and reactor shim | medium | low | One source per application; a compiler reference | 10 |
| 10 | Typed screen protocol and typed compositor | large | depends on step 0 | Faster path to the screen for every world | 10 |
| 11 | Experiment: worlds in user mode under PMP, the processor's memory protection | medium | high | Confinement of any native code | 7 |
| 12 | Linear handles, then typestate | medium to large | medium | Compile-time checking of grants and releases | 9 |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S0["0 Measure"] --> S10["10 Screen protocol and compositor"]
    S0 --> S5["5 Better RV32 backend"]
    S1["1 Cache"]
    S2["2 CJI tool off the device"]
    S3["3 Interface description"] --> S6["6 Fuel, stack bound, verifier"]
    S3 --> S8["8 Per-turn arena"]
    S3 --> S9["9 JavaScript emitter and reactor shim"]
    S3 --> S10
    S4["4 Small language additions"] --> S7["7 await"]
    S5 --> S6
    S7 --> S8
    S7 --> P["Port the remaining twelve applications"]
    S8 --> P
    S8 --> S12["12 Linear handles, typestate"]
    S6 --> W["WAMR becomes optional"]
    S11["11 PMP experiment"]
```

An arrow means that the later step needs the earlier one. Steps without arrows into them can start at any time. Three features of the ordering deserve a sentence each. Steps 0 to 4 are small and low-risk and do not depend on one another; they come first, with the measurement of step 0 run early because the larger steps 5 and 10 wait on its result. Step 7 comes before the remaining ports because of the multiplier of section 10.1: porting twelve applications in the current style would produce a great deal of code that `await` would then make obsolete. Step 10 is deliberately late and conditional.

## 10.7 Predictions that would falsify the plan

A plan built on measurements should say what further measurements would refute it. Each of the following is a specific, checkable prediction that follows from an article of this issue. Where the article gave a number, it is repeated here; where it gave only a direction, a threshold is set here so that the prediction can fail.

| Prediction | Check | If it fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A compile-time operand stack gives 593 instructions for Files, where today there are 1,529 (Article 5) | Implement it for Files first and count | The counting model is wrong; re-examine before doing Editor |
| Application code is under 10 percent of key press to pixels (Article 2's rough model gives under 5 percent of the measured part) | Step 0 | Raise the priority of step 5 for the affected application |
| With a cache, an unedited Editor costs under 100 ms at boot instead of 2–3 s (Article 6 expects 14 ms to load plus tens of milliseconds to hash) | Time a boot with a warm cache | Look at hashing and load costs |
| A verifier accepts all code the new backend emits and rejects that code after random single-bit changes, or the changed code can do no harm (Article 7, section 7.6) | Mutation testing of emitted modules | Find which property the accepted harmful module violates and add the missing check |
| The `await` transformation reproduces Editor's behaviour using no more than its current 71 state fields (Article 8, section 8.6) | Rewrite Editor's open and search paths with `await` and compare screens | Saving every variable that is live across a wait is less economical than hand-written state; examine which variables it saves that the hand-written code does not |

## 10.8 Key points

- The firmware carries three engines, two compilers, a run-time system for the first compiler's output, and three reactors. The typed ports are four to six times longer than the JavaScript they replace.
- The reactor's 28 functions are listed by hand in three files that must agree in order. One interface description should generate all three.
- Screen updates are exchanged as JSON text that one side formats and the other parses into garbage-collected objects. A typed binary protocol removes both steps; it should be built only if measurement confirms that the compositor dominates.
- A JavaScript emitter for the typed language would give one source per application and an independent reference for the compiler.
- The CJI tool should leave the device now. WAMR can become optional once native code can be verified.
- Small, low-risk steps come first; `await` comes before the remaining ports; the compositor work waits for evidence.

## 10.9 Check your understanding

1. The reactor's header stores the number of reactor functions, and the linker checks it. Which mistake does that check catch, which does it miss, and how does the proposed interface description remove both?
2. Of the five steps of a screen update in section 10.3, which three exist only because the two sides exchange text, and why do the other two remain under a binary protocol?
3. Why is deleting type annotations not sufficient to make typed source run correctly in a JavaScript engine? Give two specific constructs and what must be added for each.
4. A JavaScript emitter gives a reference implementation derived from the same source. What kind of error can it detect, and what kind can it not?
5. Why does the roadmap place `await` before porting the remaining applications? Use the figures of section 10.1 in your answer.
6. Choose one prediction from section 10.7 and state what observation would refute it and what the plan says to do then.

# Glossary

Each term is defined as it is used in this issue. The number in brackets is the article that introduces it.

## The system

**Claim** [1]. An entry in the system's manifest stating that a world may open a given kind of hardware or a given directory. The nucleus checks every such use against the world's claims.

**Compositor** [1]. The world that owns the screen. Applications send it a description of their screen; it lays the description out and draws it.

**Engine** [1]. The mechanism that executes a world's code. There are three: QuickJS (JavaScript), WAMR (WebAssembly) and native (RV32 machine code).

**Handle** [9]. A number that stands for an open file or a granted permission. Authority is exercised by presenting a handle to the nucleus.

**Manifest** [1]. The file that lists the system's worlds with their engines, memory limits, turn budgets and claims.

**Nucleus** [1]. The kernel, written in C. It schedules worlds, delivers messages and checks claims.

**Reactor** [1]. A prebuilt C module shipped in the firmware that connects a compiled application to the nucleus. Compiled code is copied into a reserved place inside it. The *shared typed reactor* serves any fully typed application.

**Slot** [5, 7]. Two meanings, distinguished by context. A *frame slot* is a fixed position in a function's stack frame. *The slot* in a reactor is the contiguous region reserved for an application's compiled RV32 code.

**Split-phase operation** [8]. An operation with a request that returns at once and a completion delivered later as a separate event.

**Token** [8]. A number returned when a split-phase operation is started and carried by the event that completes it.

**Trampoline** [7]. A fixed single-jump entry at the start of the reactor's slot, one per reactor function. Compiled native code calls reactor function *k* by jumping to the *k*-th trampoline.

**Trap** [1]. An immediate fault that ends a world's turn, raised for example by an out-of-range index or a division by zero.

**Turn** [1]. The handling of one event by one world.

**Turn budget** [1]. The longest time one uninterrupted piece of a turn may run. A world that overruns is stopped.

**World** [1]. One scheduled program: an application, a driver or a service, with its own memory limit and turn budget.

## The compilers

**CJI** [1]. The first compiler: it accepts unannotated JavaScript, infers types over the whole program, and emits RV32 machine code. Named after the book *Compiling JavaScript, Incrementally*.

**Demotion** [3]. In CJI, replacing an operation provisionally compiled as integer arithmetic by general floating-point arithmetic when the range proof fails.

**Library specialization** [3]. In CJI, generating a separate copy of a library routine for each call site, specialized to the types used there. Called *customization* in the Self literature.

**Lowering** [1, 5]. Translating a program from a higher-level form to a lower-level one; here, WebAssembly to RV32.

**Typed compiler** [1]. The second compiler: it accepts a small JavaScript-like language with declared types, emits WebAssembly in one pass, and optionally lowers that to RV32.

**Typed language** [1]. The source language of the typed compiler, with the types `i32`, `bool`, `string`, `buffer` and `record`.

## Program analysis

**Abstract interpretation** [3]. The general theory of analyses that compute approximate facts about all executions of a program by iterating over an ordered set of facts.

**Constraint graph** [4]. A graph with a node for each value and an edge wherever one value's facts feed another's.

**Dense and sparse analysis** [4]. A dense analysis keeps facts for every variable at every program point. A sparse analysis attaches each fact to the definition of a value and propagates it only to that value's uses.

**Demand-driven analysis** [4]. An analysis that starts from a question (for example, "is this check redundant?") and computes only what is needed to answer it.

**Fixpoint** [3]. The state of an iterative analysis in which a further visit to the program changes nothing.

**Join** [3]. The operation that combines the facts arriving at a control-flow merge. For ranges, the join of [0, 3] and [2, 9] is [0, 9].

**Jump function** [4]. For one argument of one call, a small expression giving the argument's value in terms of the enclosing function's own parameters. A form of summary.

**Liveness** [8]. A variable is live at a point if some path from that point reads it before writing it.

**Local checking** [4]. Checking and compiling a function from its own text and the declared signatures of what it calls, with no facts about its callers.

**Range (interval)** [3]. The smallest and largest value a variable can take, in CJI with flags for fraction, negative zero and NaN.

**SSA form** [4]. Static single-assignment form: a program representation in which every variable is assigned in exactly one place, with φ-functions selecting between definitions at merges. *Extended* SSA adds a renaming (π) on each outcome of a branch.

**Strongly connected component** [4]. A maximal group of nodes in a graph that all depend on each other through cycles.

**Summary** [4]. A compact description of how a function's outputs depend on its inputs.

**Whole-program inference** [3]. Solving for types or other facts using every function and every call in the program.

**Widening** [3]. Jumping a bound that keeps moving to a much larger value so that iteration terminates, at some cost in precision.

## Code generation

**Back-edge** [7]. The jump from the end of a loop body back to the loop's start.

**Branch over a jump** [5]. A conditional branch that skips an unconditional jump, used where the distance to the target is not known to be short.

**Compile-time operand stack** [5]. A list kept by the compiler during translation that records where each operand-stack value currently is: in a register, a known constant, the current value of a local, or a pending comparison. Also called a value stack, a virtual stack, or static stack caching.

**Flush** [5]. Moving every pending entry of the compile-time operand stack to a fixed, agreed location before control flow splits or merges, or before a call.

**Frame** [5]. A function's private area of memory on the stack. In Article 8, also the fixed group of persistent fields that holds an asynchronous function's saved state.

**Join (control flow)** [5]. A point in the code reached from two or more paths.

# Answers to "Check your understanding" (section 10.9)

## 1. What the count check catches and misses

The stored count catches a function that was added to the compiler's table (or to the C/assembly side) and not to the other side, because then the two lengths differ and the linker's comparison fails. It does not catch two lists that have the same length but list the functions in a different order: the count still matches, yet native code jumping to entry *k* lands on the wrong function and passes arguments with the wrong meanings. A single interface description removes both, because the compiler's table, the assembly trampolines and the C prototypes would all be *generated* from one file instead of being typed out by hand, so neither the number nor the order can drift. That is also a gain in kind, not just in degree: the current check is a length check, while generation cannot produce a disagreement at all.

Confidence: 4

## 2. Which screen-update steps exist only because of text

Steps 1, 2 and 4 exist only because the two sides exchange text: the application formatting a JSON description, the reactor converting UTF-16 to UTF-8 and adding JSON escapes, and the compositor parsing that text into a tree of heap-allocated objects. Step 3, the nucleus copying the message into the compositor's queue, remains because the application and the compositor are separate worlds with separate memory, so *something* must be passed between them, text or not. Step 5, the compositor walking the structure, computing positions and drawing, remains because that is the compositor's actual job; a binary protocol only changes the form of what it walks.

Confidence: 4

## 3. Why deleting annotations is not enough

Deleting annotations leaves JavaScript, and JavaScript's arithmetic and string behaviour differ from the typed language's, so the program would compute different answers rather than merely look different. Two examples: `a + b` on `i32` wraps at 32 bits in the typed language but is 64-bit floating-point addition in JavaScript, so the emitter must add `(a + b) | 0`; and `a * b` on `i32` wraps while JavaScript multiplication can lose low bits above 2⁵³, so the emitter must use `Math.imul(a, b)`. Two further cases from the article's table: `a / b` on `i32` truncates and traps on zero instead of giving a fraction or infinity (a checked helper is needed), and `s.charCodeAt(i)` out of range traps instead of returning NaN (a wrapper class with a checked method is needed). `record` declarations have no JavaScript equivalent either and must become objects or typed arrays.

Confidence: 4

## 4. What a JavaScript-emitter reference can and cannot detect

Because it is a second, independent implementation of the language's semantics, it can detect errors in the WebAssembly and RV32 backends: run an application through both paths and compare the screens, and a disagreement points at one of the two backends. It can also be used without a hand-written JavaScript original, which is what makes it a cheap reference. It cannot detect an error in the source program's own logic, because a fault in the typed source appears in both implementations and cancels out. The article states this limit explicitly and adds that during a port the original JavaScript application must stay the standard of behaviour.

Confidence: 4

## 5. Why `await` comes before the remaining ports

Section 10.1 shows that typed ports are much longer than the JavaScript they replace: Editor is 316 lines of JavaScript against about 1,730 lines of typed source (5.5 times), and Agenda is 307 lines against 468 lines of typed source plus 869 lines of C (1,337 lines, 4.4 times). The article attributes that price to missing language features, including the absence of `await`, which forces hand-written continuations. With twelve applications still to port, doing the ports first would generate a large body of code that a later `await` would make obsolete. Adding `await` first (roadmap step 7) therefore shrinks the work of the remaining ports; this is why the arrow runs from step 7 to "Port the remaining twelve applications".

Confidence: 4

## 6. One prediction and what would refute it

Take the prediction that a compile-time operand stack gives 593 instructions for Files where there are today 1,529. The refuting observation is a count above 593 after implementing the compile-time operand stack for Files first; a count of, say, 1,100 would mean the saving is far smaller than claimed. The plan then says the counting model is wrong and must be re-examined before the same change is attempted on Editor. Note the prediction is deliberately ordered: Files is the cheap trial that protects the larger application from a bad model.

Confidence: 4

# Reader feedback on "10. Architecture and a Roadmap"

Read as a reader of the series: article.md front to back, with glossary.md consulted for every
term I did not already know. Notes below are only where the text failed to teach.

## Passages I had to read twice

1. "The number of functions is also stored in a header at the start of the reactor's code area, and the linker compares it with the length of the compiler's table."
   — I could not tell how a linker learns the length of a table that lives in a JavaScript file, or whether the assembly file's list is checked at all. The sentence is doing the work of the whole argument in 10.2 and it hides the mechanism.

2. "Article 2 presented evidence that the compositor is the largest consumer of time on the path to the screen, and noted that in the measured firmware it was already native code."
   — "already native" reads like a contradiction of the next paragraph, which treats the compositor as slow JavaScript. Only after finishing 10.3 do you see that "native" means "compiled by CJI, with CJI's garbage collector and text parsing still in it".

3. "The typed versions are four to six times longer than the programs they replace: a factor of 5.5 for Editor, and 4.4 for Agenda when its C reactor is counted."
   — "when its C reactor is counted" is the load-bearing clause: without the 869 lines of C, Agenda's typed source is only 468/307 ≈ 1.5 times longer. The multiplier is therefore a claim about a *counting convention*, and the convention is stated only once, in passing, in a parenthesis.

4. "Application code is under 10 percent of key press to pixels (Article 2's rough model gives under 5 percent of the measured part)"
   — two percentages with no sign of how they relate. Is the 5 percent a subset of the 10 percent? Which one would the measurement of step 0 test?

5. "CJI remains valuable as a workstation compiler that turns existing JavaScript worlds into native code for the firmware image."
   — "workstation compiler" appears nowhere else, and this is the pivot of the whole "take CJI off the device" decision, so the alternative role is described in half a sentence.

6. "Steps 0 to 4 are small and low-risk and do not depend on one another; they come first, with the measurement of step 0 run early because the larger steps 5 and 10 wait on its result."
   — But the diagram draws an arrow from 5 to 6 and from 4 to 7, so "do not depend on one another" and the figure need to be reconciled by the reader (the sentence only covers 0–4; I read it as covering more on the first pass).

## Terms used before they were explained, or never explained

- **code unit** (10.1 "no string operations beyond single code units"; 10.3 "17 rows of at most 49 characters. As 16-bit code units…"). Never defined; the glossary has no entry, and the whole byte count in 10.3 rests on it.
- **guard facts** (10.6, step 4: "guard facts for bounds checks"). Never explained anywhere; not in the glossary.
- **static stack bound** (10.6, step 6). Never explained; presumably the Article 7 stack-safety point, but the article does not say so.
- **mutation testing** (10.7, verifier prediction: "Mutation testing of emitted modules"). Never explained; not in the glossary, yet it is the stated way to falsify the central safety claim.
- **forward calls with a cycle check** (10.6, step 4). Never explained; I do not know what a cycle check protects against.
- **garbage collector / garbage-collected heap** (10.1 CJI runtime row; 10.3 step 4). Used as if known; no glossary entry, though the cost argument depends on it.
- **dynamic values** (10.1, CJI runtime row; 10.4 "the interpreter would still treat every number as a general value"). No glossary entry.
- **linker** (10.2). Assumed background; not in the glossary and no explanation of what it links here.
- **relocated at boot** (10.1, CJI compiler tool row; 10.6 step 2 "a boot-time relocation that had to be scheduled around"). Never explained, yet it is offered as a reason to delete a component.
- **16 KiB message limit** (10.3 step 3). Stated as fact with no definition of where the limit lives (protocol, queue, or buffer).
- **WIT** is *not* on this list: 10.2 explains it ("The WebAssembly Component Model's interface language") and the glossary covers the Component Model's neighbours. Nor are *fuel*, *trampoline*, *handle*, *verifier*, *arena*, *continuation*, *state machine* — all in the glossary.

## Claims I could not verify from the article itself

1. "The design notes budget up to six output bytes per input unit for this step" and later "The figure of six bytes per unit in step 2 is from the Editor's capacity design note in the project's records."
   — The note is never cited, quoted or linked; the same claim is asserted twice with no evidence. A reader cannot check whether six is a real bound or an exaggeration chosen to make text look expensive.

2. "Its build times of minutes make it unusable interactively, and it costs 660 kB and a boot-time relocation that had to be scheduled around."
   — No measurement is given for build time (which program? which hardware?), and 660 kB is stated without a build log or a way to reproduce it. This is the stated reason for roadmap step 2, the only step the article says can be done "now".

3. "The typed versions are four to six times longer than the programs they replace."
   — The Editor figure can be checked (1730/316 = 5.47) and Agenda's can be checked (468 + 869 = 1337, 1337/307 = 4.35), but the article never says whether C reactor lines *should* count as typed source. Without that rule the multiplier — the article's main argument for extending the language — is a choice, not a measurement.

4. "The project's device-language study considered compiling the typed language to JavaScript as the way to *run applications fast*, and rejected it for that purpose, because the interpreter would still treat every number as a general value."
   — The study is never described or cited. Since this passage pre-empts the obvious objection to 10.4, the reader needs at least where the study is and what it measured.

5. "A message is limited to 16 KiB" (10.3 step 3) and "A full Editor screen is 17 rows of at most 49 characters."
   — The second is checkable against the byte arithmetic (I get 833 × 2 = 1,666 bytes of text plus 17 × 4 = 68 bytes of headers = 1,734, which matches). The first has no source, and it is the constraint that decides whether the binary protocol even fits, so it matters.

6. "It is the one world whose speed every other world's responsiveness depends on."
   — Stated of the compositor with no measurement; the whole of step 10 is conditional on exactly this, and section 10.7 assigns the evidence to Article 2, which this article does not summarise numerically ("largest consumer of time" is not a figure).

7. "This is ordinary practice wherever two languages meet."
   — A general claim about industry practice with one example (WIT). It matters because it is offered in place of an argument for the interface description.

8. "Native code about 2.7 times smaller" (10.6, step 5).
   — No working shown here and the 2.7 is not derived from anything in this article; a reader must trust Article 5.

9. "When the typed compiler fails or is disabled, the firmware falls back to the original JavaScript application."
   — No description of how that fallback is chosen or triggered, so "the two can drift apart" cannot be evaluated.

## Section scores

- **10.1 What the firmware contains — 4.** The tables are concrete and the size figures give a foothold, but the length multiplier hides its counting rule and two terms (dynamic values, garbage collector) go undefined in the very row that costs the most.
- **10.2 One description of the reactor's functions — 3.** The failure mode (same length, different order) is explained well, but the mechanics of the existing check, and so of the fix, stay vague, and the WIT paragraph adds three new terms in one sentence.
- **10.3 A typed screen protocol — 4.** The five-step walkthrough is the clearest passage in the article and the byte arithmetic checks out; the "already native" sentence at the start works against it.
- **10.4 One source for both engines — 4.** The table of rewrites is excellent and the stated limit (a reference cannot catch source errors) is honest; the asm.js and TypeScript paragraphs are background the reader cannot check and one of them (the device-language study) is an appeal to an uncited document.
- **10.5 Fewer engines — 3.** The table of "needed as long as / could be removed when" is a good form, but the decision rests on "workstation compiler" and on build times that are asserted, not shown.
- **10.6 The roadmap — 3.** The table and graph are genuinely useful, but several steps are named with undefined terms (guard facts, static stack bound, cycle check), "small/medium/large" time classes are not tied to any observed task, and the figure contradicts the prose unless read carefully.
- **10.7 Predictions that would falsify the plan — 3.** The idea is admirable and the checks are specific; but four of the five rows depend on numbers from other articles that this article does not restate or derive, and the second row sets two thresholds (10 percent, 5 percent) without saying how they relate.
- **10.8 Key points — 4.** Accurate and compresses the sections well; it is nearly a second summary of the article, which is fine at the end of a series but repeats rather than adds.
- **10.9 Check your understanding — 4.** The questions are answerable and each maps to a section; none asked for a number that is not in the text.

## Questions that the article did not let me answer

All six were answerable in substance, but two only partly:

- **Question 1** is answerable as far as "catches a length mismatch, misses a reordering". What I could not get from the text is *how* the count check is performed (where the compiler's table length comes from at link time) and whether the assembly file is length-checked at all. So I can say what the check misses but not quite why the check is what it is.
- **Question 2** is answerable because the article labels steps 3 and 5 as remaining; but the reason "this step would remain with any protocol" is given for step 3 only, and for step 5 the reader must supply the reasoning ("that is the compositor's actual job" is stated in parentheses, which is enough, but barely).
- **Question 6** is answerable in form, but a reader who wants to know *why* 593 is the right number cannot find it here; only the instruction "implement it for Files first and count".

## One thing to add and one thing to cut

**Add:** one worked example carried all the way through — a single reactor function shown as a row of the compiler's table, its trampoline in `rv32-slot.S`, and its C prototype in `world.c`, then the same function in the proposed interface description, plus one row of a screen record written by the application and read by the compositor. Section 10.2's argument is entirely about files that must agree in order, and the reader never sees even one line of them; a dozen lines of real text would turn the central proposal from a description into something I could check and picture. It would also show what "which capability the function requires" and "how much fuel a call is charged" look like as fields.

**Cut:** the repeated six-bytes-per-unit sentence in 10.3 ("The figure of six bytes per unit in step 2 is from the Editor's capacity design note in the project's records"). Step 2 already says the design notes budget six bytes per input unit; restating the figure four sentences later, with the same missing citation, adds length without adding evidence — and the space is better spent on the one example above.
